title: Cooperation (the fall book list)
content:
Last week’s book list was a success, and I realized that it would work even better with others. Bookstores work precisely because they stack the books right next to each other.

[![Image 1](https://i0.wp.com/seths.blog/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Screenshot-2026-10-27-at-8.06.21-AM.jpg?resize=888%2C1024&ssl=1)](https://thehotlist.org/)
Even though each of these authors has a book out this fall, they’re not my competition. Too often, we avoid cooperation because we’re embracing scarcity.

Each of us will be linking to [thehotlist.org](https://www.thehotlist.org/) today. Ideas that spread, win. The page automatically updates based on which books get clicked on the most.

What happens when you help connect and organize the others?

title: Can You Recognize the Subject of This Year’s Microscopic Photography Contest Winner?
content:
The Nikon Small World photography contest doesn’t celebrate [weather](https://nautil.us/these-are-the-most-stunning-weather-photos-of-the-year-1286043), [wildlife](https://nautil.us/the-wildlife-photo-of-the-year-may-break-your-heart-1285913), or [natural landscapes](https://nautil.us/check-out-the-natural-beauty-of-the-natural-landscape-photography-awards-1285755). Instead, it’s meant to honor images of the world at the smallest possible scales, offering unique perspectives on the details of the environments around us.

This year, judges cited 76 of the 1,803 entries as either an award winner, runner-up, honorable mention, or image of distinction.

[The contest’s mission](https://www.nikonsmallworld.com/news/nikon-small-world-celebrates-50-years-of-microscopic-marvels) is to “showcase the beauty and complexity of things seen through the microscope,” and this year’s winners definitely fulfilled that promise. There was everything from inkjet printers and pens, to wasps and neurons—all in high resolution and ultra close-up (but of course).

German Ole Bielfeldt won first place for his shot of the inner workings of an inkjet printer. Getting the final photograph involved a custom printing rig and a custom microscopic camera rig, using a 20x magnification. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

Second place went to John-Oliver Dum, also from Germany, who used a 20x magnification to grab this image of a jumping spider (Salticus scenicus) with particles of pollen on it. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

For the third-place photo, Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery employed 5x magnification to show neurons in an expanded mouse brain. Both work at the Allen Institute in Seattle. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

I bet you can’t you guess what this is: the very tip of a ballpoint pen, snapped at 20x magnification by Justin Theodore Benttinen from the U.S. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

The inner structure of a closed daisy, captured at 10x magnification by Michael Crutchley of the U.K., using a darkfield microscopic photography technique to foreground the flower. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

Another one where it might take you a minute to figure out what you’re looking at: a Hemitrichia slime mold spore structure, taken at a 10x magnification, by Eric Epstein of the U.S. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

These are human neurons reprogrammed from skin cells, growing in a microfluidic chamber. The image, photographed at 20x magnification, is the work of Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol, from Augusta University in Georgia. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

It looks like some sort of alien, but this is actually pencil lead (at the top) being exposed to a high-voltage electrical discharge. The photograph, at 10x magnification, is by Dr. Marcel Clemens from Italy. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

Courtesy of Dr. Francisco Lázaro-Diéguez from the Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York, this is a 40x-magnification image of a dedifferentiated liver endothelial cell from the lining of a blood vessel. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

A parasitoid wasp (Conura sp.) pulling itself out of a butterfly chrysalis (Opsiphanes sp.) after using it for food, as shot by Michael Parra Puentes from Colombia at 3.7x magnification. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

A ghostly image of a 20-day-old sea urchin larva, lit up by blue fluorescent nuclei, taken at 20x magnification. The photographer behind it is Svenja Carolin Kling, working for the Scripps Institution of Oceanography. _Credit: Nikon Small World_

title: Ketamine’s Role in Alleged Cornell Rape Highlights Flood of Psychoactive Drugs on Campus
content:
Former Cornell student Jane Doe, who[filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026](https://www.cornellsun.com/article/2026/09/tccsuykuvb4z)alleging that seven fraternity members raped her at a party, said the young men who assaulted her pressured her into taking the drug ketamine.

As an[emergency room physician, medical toxicologist](https://med.virginia.edu/emergency-medicine/faculty/full-time-faculty/christopher-p-holstege-md/)and the[head of student health services](https://studentaffairs.virginia.edu/staff/christopher-holstege)at the University of Virginia, I have had a front-row seat to the growing danger that psychoactive substances such as ketamine present to the health and safety of university students.

[Ketamine and its emerging spin-off versions](https://med.virginia.edu/toxicology/wp-content/uploads/sites/268/2026/03/Mar26-Ketamine-analogues.pdf)are part of a[wave of new and evolving designer drugs](https://www.unodc.org/unodc/secured/wdr/wdr2013/World_Drug_Report_2013.pdf)entering the United States and other countries. How widely these substances are used remains unknown, since most hospitals are[unable to detect them](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.emc.2022.01.003)on standard urine drug screens. But[ketamine and other drugs](https://www.justice.gov/archive/ndic/pubs8/8872/index.htm#commission)are being increasingly reported as[agents used in sexual assault](https://doi.org/10.28933/ijprr-2021-07-1505)– either when people take these drugs voluntarily, are pressured to take them or are given them covertly.

The increasing prevalence of ketamine and other drugs—and their use in sexual assault—is[playing out on college campuses across the U.S.](https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.focus.20180037)and putting students at risk.

## A Growing Supply

Ketamine is a synthetic chemical that was[first synthesized in 1962](https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/health-and-medicine/ketamine/). The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it as a[general anesthetic for people and animals](https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2016.00612)in 1970, and doctors and veterinarians used it for decades to induce anesthesia during surgeries and to relieve pain.

People have[used ketamine recreationally](https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9798894551944.lg03)since the 1970s. Getting high on it became more popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, when it was called “Special K.” It was frequently found in the club drug scenes and was associated with raves into the 1990s. Today, ketamine is sold on the street under a[variety of slang names](https://www.justice.gov/archive/ndic/pubs8/8872/8872p.pdf), such as K, Ket, and Vitamin K.

In 2019,[the FDA approved a nasal spray version of ketamine](https://doi.org/10.1017/S2045796019000751), called esketamine, to treat depression that does not respond to other treatments. That drug’s use is tightly regulated, but clinicians are increasingly prescribing ketamine “off-label” for a variety of psychiatric conditions, including[post-traumatic stress disorder](https://theconversation.com/ketamine-can-rapidly-reduce-symptoms-of-ptsd-and-depression-new-study-finds-216077).

Cases of poisoning caused by ketamine in the U.S.[doubled between 2019 and 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2025.112549), according to an analysis of calls to poison control centers nationwide, and are now the highest they’ve ever been. This surge is in part due to the more widespread medical use of ketamine, which makes accessing it much easier. But[street versions of the drug](https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2023.1423)are also prevalent as chemists in basement laboratories create novel ketamine analogs.

## Ketamine’s Effects on the Body

Ketamine’s effects vary depending on the dose and the person. It can cause someone to dissociate, creating an altered state of consciousness, changing what’s perceived through the senses and causing a sense of detachment from one’s self and one’s surroundings. The drug can also[cause coma at high doses](https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/special-subjects/illicit-drugs-and-intoxicants/ketamine-and-phencyclidine).

Someone who orally consumes ketamine would typically begin to[feel its effects within 20 minutes](https://doi.org/10.1080/20961790.2017.1285219). If they inhale or inject it, the effects are almost immediate. The primary effects generally wear off in less than an hour, but a person’s senses may remain dulled and their judgment and coordination impaired for several hours afterward.

Ketamine can cause a slew of other side effects, including delirium, amnesia, increased salivation, abnormal eye movements, high blood pressure and potentially fatal breathing problems. Alcohol and other drugs can[interact with ketamine to worsen these effects](https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms23147800)significantly.

Ketamine is generally sold illegally as either a colorless, odorless liquid or a white or off-white powder. Either form can be easily and covertly placed into an unsuspecting person’s beverage or food. Ketamine can be snorted, and it can be smoked or vaped on products such as marijuana.

## Ketamine and Other Drugs in Sexual Assault

Research is extremely spotty on how often a perpetrator of rape or sexual assault[uses a chemical agent](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.emc.2007.02.008)—whether ketamine, alcohol or another substance—to alter a victim’s senses. Research suggests that most often both parties[use mind-altering substances voluntarily](https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/108860), although the effects of these substances can alter a person’s ability to grant consent.

Even so, there are numerous reports of perpetrators spiking a victim’s drink or otherwise slipping a drug to them without their knowledge. According to one study,[4.2% of rape victims were drugged covertly](https://www.ojp.gov/library/publications/estimate-incidence-drug-facilitated-sexual-assault-us-final-report), though how often this actually happens is undoubtedly underreported.

That’s because it’s very hard to detect drugs taken this way. Most of the substances used to facilitate sexual assaults are rapidly absorbed and metabolized by the body, rendering them difficult to detect in routine urine and blood drug screenings. Another issue is that many days may have elapsed between the victim ingesting the drugs and their subsequent treatment at a medical facility.

Victims of rape or sexual assault are often reluctant to report incidents because of a sense of embarrassment, guilt or perceived responsibility, or because they may know their attacker. Some may[not trust that their institution or local law enforcement](https://theconversation.com/handling-of-rape-allegations-at-cornell-shows-why-so-many-assaults-go-unreported-victims-dont-trust-the-institutions-that-are-supposed-to-help-them-293907)will support them.

In my experience, the involvement of ketamine or other drugs invariably makes a bad situation worse—complicating consent, impairing judgment and reducing inhibitions.[Ketamine causes confusion and drowsiness](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.emc.2007.02.008), and its sedative, hypnotic and memory-erasing properties can diminish a survivor’s recollection of events surrounding the sexual assault.

The availability of these drugs in the U.S., including on college campuses, has risen sharply—particularly since the early 2010s, as a slew of new substances have emerged and[international drug control efforts have not kept up](https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.14236). Without more active education and prevention efforts, as well as better detection methods for these drugs, students will continue to pay the price. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Our Planet’s Lungs Are Suffering
content:
The Amazon Rainforest is often referred to as the “lungs of the planet” because its lush canopy “inhales” carbon dioxide and “exhales” oxygen. This breathing pattern is part of an important natural defense against climate change, pulling carbon from the atmosphere and sequestering it, but that might be changing. According to a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-11168-1) in _Nature_, the Amazon may shift from a net sink to a net source of atmospheric carbon.

A team of climate scientists arrived at that conclusion after analyzing atmospheric samples taken by planes criss-crossing the skies over the Amazon for 15 years. Satellite-based monitoring is difficult because of the dense blanket of cloud cover generated by [evaporating moisture](https://nautil.us/the-amazon-river-in-the-sky-312496) and ground-based systems are few and far between. So the team went straight to the source.

**Read more: “[The Rainforest Is Teeming with Consciousness](https://nautil.us/the-rainforest-is-teeming-with-consciousness-237602)”**

“In this context, airborne vertical profiling fills a critical gap, providing the most direct way to quantify the movement of carbon between tropical land ecosystems and the atmosphere at the regional scale,” study author Jen Johnson of the University of Kansas explained in a [statement](https://news.ku.edu/news/article/study-finds-amazon-rainforest-now-releases-more-carbon-than-it-absorbs).

The team divided the15 years studied into three different groups: wet periods with little human interference, periods of heavy deforestation but minimal climate stressors, and periods marked by acute climate stress (droughts, wildfires, and El Niños).

“We wanted to know, ‘Is the effect of global climate on the Amazon the most important factor determining its carbon balance, or are regional human-driven activities—like deforestation and clearing through wildfires—equally or more important?’” Johnson said.

The team found that during wet years, when the forests were left relatively unperturbed, the Amazon was a net source of carbon, but just a small one. Things got much worse in other years. Carbon emissions spiked during years when the climate was mild but deforestation increased. Years where high levels of human activity and climate stressors coincided were the worst of all.

In other words, whether it’s from wildfires or deforestation, human activity is transforming the Amazon from a net carbon sink into a net carbon source with potentially disastrous consequences for climate change.

“For many decades, there has been concern about the idea of a tipping point, where gradual drying and gradual loss of the forest could feed back on itself in a self-reinforcing way,” Johnson said. “That could create a transition from an ecosystem type that has stored huge amounts of carbon in living vegetation to drier forests or other ecosystem types that do not store nearly as much carbon.”

The solution, per Johnson, is relatively simple: stop destroying the trees. “Measures to bring deforestation down to zero are required to manage net carbon emissions from the Amazon,” she said.

The alternative is finding out how to live on a planet suffering from chronic lung disease. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Dear Human, Poetry Might Save Us from the Apocalypse
content:
_When we tell the story  
of how we survived the collapse,  
we might say:  
like birds, we learned  
to move as one.  
We grew lighter  
and lengthened our wings._

These are the final lines of “[Dear Human at the Edge of Time](https://dearhuman.poetsforscience.org/community-poem/): A Community Poem.” Assembled from the contributions of 14 different writers across the United States, the poem tells a story about the future that is simultaneously devastating and hopeful.

In the three years since the poem was penned, the question of how we might collectively survive collapse has become an increasingly pressing one. It turns out, we are not paying enough attention to the birds. We have not learned to move as one.

The poem was published in 2023 by [Poets for Science](https://poetsforscience.org/) in connection with the Fifth National Climate [Assessment](https://toolkit.climate.gov/NCA5), which revealed that climate change was already ravaging every region of the United States through rising temperatures, punishing drought, savage wildfires, and deadly storms.

**Read more: “[Poetry Gives Us Power](https://nautil.us/poetry-gives-us-power-1210597)”**

But humanity continues to fall short of the change needed to keep the Earth on a safe course for future generations. The data on climate change have told a clear story for a long time, but that story is not getting through.

Could art and poetry dedicated to conservation themes help ignite a greater feeling of urgency about our predicament and map a way forward? Poets for Science, forged in the turmoil of the first Trump administration, has made this call to action one of its missions.

The group is uniting poets and scientists in collaborations that aim to make the science of conservation both felt viscerally and understood intellectually. It’s also inviting the public to participate with verse or other creative work of their own.

The poem “Dear Human” lives on an interactive [platform](https://sparkpoems.com/dear-human/share) that allows anyone to contribute. Writers can respond to poems published in an award-winning climate poetry [anthology](https://palomapress.org/dear-human/), add to a digital gallery of climate art, or build their own “found poems” out of text borrowed from the Fifth National Climate Assessment.

“Why not poetry?” says poet David Hassler, who co-founded Poets for Science together with American nature poet Jane Hirshfield in 2017. In just a couple of weeks, Poets for Science will hold its first in-person [gathering](https://poetsforscience.org/gathering-2026/), where scientists and poets will meet across three days to explore the connections between their disciplines, and ways to inspire the civic imagination. That meeting is sponsored by the Wick Poetry Center at Kent State University in Ohio, which Hassler directs.

I spoke with Hassler recently about how poetry is like lichen—and how it can help make science meaningful while inspiring collective action.  
**There have been many periods across history when art and science were closely aligned. Artists were scientists and scientists were artists. Nobel laureate neuroscientist Eric Kandel beautifully describes such a [period](https://nautil.us/gustav-klimt-in-the-brain-lab-237324) in Vienna at the turn of the 20th century in his book****_The Age of Insight_. The Renaissance, too, was packed with figures who merged artistic mastery with scientific inquiry. But during the scientific revolution, art and science split. There was this intellectual [divide](https://nautil.us/who-said-science-and-art-were-two-cultures-238351). Today it seems like the pendulum might be swinging back the other way. What do you make of this shift?**

Yes, all these collective efforts have been co-arising all around the globe, people pursuing similar intersections of science and humanities and arts. It’s what we have discovered in pulling together this Poets for Science gathering. You know, we’re not alone. When we started Poetry for Science in 2017, we were tapping into a collective nerve that I think is shared by so many people. And it’s really been growing over the past 10 to 15 years.

In a recent interview, I was reminded that the word “scientist” was coined in the mid 1800s. Before that, they were “natural philosophers.” There’s this divide between our belief that over here’s my rational thinking, and over there’s my emotional thinking. Here’s my scientific inquiry and over there’s my creative expression.

This divide has been exacerbated by our biases and our technology. I think that it has come to a breaking point, where people are hungering to integrate facts with feelings, so that what we’re learning through the facts of science has meaning in our lives, emotionally and in our lived experience. Perhaps this need to be intentional about bringing them back together in conversation has happened out of an awareness of our failure at progress. We’re feeling sicker. We’re feeling more divided, more alone, more unhealthy, and there’s been a kind of quiet desperation.

We’re also looking for creative solutions to intractable problems in our collective lives and AI is making us question what it means to be human. There’s this attack on the humanities, and tech bros are saying we just need to be good bots. Maybe there’s a moment here where we’re infusing the arts back into our rational scientific thinking because we need to remind ourselves what it means to be human and what we value about being human. Scientists are trying to remember that the questions they ask and the work they do is informed by their humanness, by their cultural background, their emotional lives, their beliefs, their lived experience.

**Do you think that poetry does something for science or for public understanding of science that other art forms can’t?**

I think all art forms can help us make meaning and carry grief and hold our sense of awe and to use that as an energy source, to contain it and to give it shape. All art can do that.

But here’s what poetry can do: It can take the natural metaphors of science and highlight them. We’re not inventing them. If I say that we’re having a “mycelial” conversation, you know what I mean, because we now understand how a mycorrhizal network in soil helps trees communicate with each other and share signals of nurture, but also warning, through this fungal network, this mycorrhizal network.

I think that the language we use to describe the world not only influences how we behave toward the world, it truly influences what we’re able to actually see in the world. The root word of science means to know from Latin, and I think the economy of language in a poem helps us carry new knowledge into the world. And that’s gone a long way. We have been told over and over again that poets are now feeling inspired and getting prompts for their writing from scientific articles and using the language of science in their poems.

But it’s working both ways. Scientists are saying they’re turning to poetry. We have so many poems on the poetsforscience.org global gallery and in this anthology [_The Nature of Our Times_](https://palomapress.org/the-nature-of-our-times/) written by scientists. Why? They say that they don’t have a place in their scientific paper or essay to put their emotional language. The poems offer a place to put their awe and grief and fear. Many scientists also say they’re using the arts and humanities to help them shape the questions they ask and the directions they go in their scientific inquiry. Laura Valski, for instance, talks about how in her research with ecology [in Washington State], she’s attuned to the stories of the native people of that region and of the language they use to inform the questions she asks.

**I love what Jane Hirshfield says, that the metaphor and the microscope are both instruments of discovery.**

Yes, metaphor stems from _metapheran_ in Greek, its origin. It means to carry, to cross over. In a sense, we’re carrying new knowledge over from science into our emotional lives through language and metaphor. And that’s how it can bring change.

**Obviously, science is many things. Not just conservation, but also technology, so it’s AI and surveillance cameras, or it’s building weapons.**

Yes, and some kinds of poetry are used by dictators to influence mass crowds and to hypnotize people. The spell of poetry can be used for good and for bad. So can science. Both of them are that powerful.

**How do you grapple with this darker side of science and poetry when you encourage collaborations?**

The 14th century poet Rumi said your intention does all the work. We do it with care and with the right intention and with rigor and with honesty. I’m not writing a poem to influence your behavior for my gain. I’m writing a poem because I have an intention to speak a truth that is authentic to me. The paradox is that if I can speak authentically and truthfully about my own idiosyncratic personal life, only then can it have a power that speaks to others and help them find their own meaning from it.

So, yes, we can create nuclear weapons and toxic chemicals. I just watched this frightening documentary about the pesticides that we’re using in agriculture that are destroying our soil, our health, and our bodies. Those chemicals were invented by a German scientist for warfare in World War II. The companies literally took the research that was being done for warfare and tweaked it to use on our crops. How’s that for an image?

**In the essay you write that art without science risks inspiring ineffective action. Why is that?**

If I don’t understand how mycelial networks actually work and I wanna write a poem about mycelium, then perhaps what I’m writing might work as a poem, but it doesn’t help me understand the forest and act in ways that create the conditions for that forest to thrive. We have a crisis of science communication, which was the origin of the Poets for Science movement in 2017, so poems can help us make meaning and speak to our own lived experience and our emotional lives. And by doing that, to make meaning of science.

This Poets for Science initiative began in response to the actions of the first Trump administration, and out of desperation, anger, grief, and fear. Jane Hirshfield wrote a poem, and that poem went around the world essentially in 2017. And then she called me, and said, “Can you help me?” And I said, “Of course.” And our design team put together 23 seven-foot banners of poems about science that she curated. We went to the National Mall for the very first March for Science on Earth Day. Poets for Science had a teach-in tent. There was never room for anybody to sit because it was constantly full the whole day.

**What do successful poems about conservation like Hirshfield’s get right?**

I avoid rating this poem over that poem and saying this poem succeeds and that poem fails. I go back to the intention of the poet and the context in which the poem is presented. I work a lot in the schools with fourth graders and eighth graders and I’ve seen the work of poems happen. We write poems to change ourselves. The poem becomes a kind of residue, it marks a new insight.

The poems that seem to translate the experience of the poet to another listener use metaphors grounded in authentic truth. The language has specificity to it. The metaphor works at multiple levels. The figurative language accurately describes or points to, for instance, how root systems in the soil communicate and support one another toward the collective health of a forest. Ideally, this language has the vibrancy of a true conversation, which from Latin “conveyor” means “together to turn.” We forget when reading where your idea ends and my idea begins. We’re caught up in this decentralized collective effort to move an idea further or to hit upon phrasing for an expression.

**Are there poems either from****_The Nature of Our Times_****or otherwise, that you feel meaningfully changed a conservation outcome? Or would you not measure it in that way?**

There’s a great phrase that Jane Hirshfield used: She says perhaps poems are the lichens of activism. And one of the things about lichens is that the work they’re doing is often very, very, very slow, often subtle, and often unseen. I think the same can be true of poems. It’s not so easy to say, “Ah, two weeks later, you changed your behavior.” And there’s something about the arts and poetry that resists scientific inquiry.

So this is also pushing against a tension that I think is interesting. So many questions of the spirit are not answerable or provable. Donald Hall says, “Poems are the unsayable said.” What he’s pointing at is the tyranny of what we can measure. Rebecca Solnit talks about this. We can be tyrannized by only believing in what we can absolutely measure. And then suddenly, we’re feeling deprived of spiritual life, because that’s what we can’t measure.

I think poems flirt with that notion of “let’s be patient like lichen. Let’s be tolerant of things that don’t have an easy answer.” Maybe the work of lichens is that work of breaking rocks, slowly making soil. It’s the creative, productive work of decomposition. There’s an element of poems breaking our rigid ways of thinking and feeling and opening up new possibilities that we don’t quite fit into yet. We don’t know when that’s gonna change our behavior. We never quite are certain about it. But they’re pulling us in and they’re making us pause. And in that pause, we suddenly have room for new thought or for making a connection we would never have made before or for simply questioning a very rigid way of thinking that we always carried for so long.

**Towards the end of the essay, you suggest that we need research into which kinds of artistic approaches and collaborations could have real impact.**

What I’m saying is take caution. Research with patience. This is not supposed to be easy. We don’t need to be overly ambitious. James Pennebaker’s research from 30 years ago about journaling and the power of using language to process grief, it moved the needle. It wasn’t overshooting in its statements. How do we find the appropriate way to engage in research that can bring other people into the conversation? We’re a small group, the world of poets. Talk about a bubble. Nobody inside it needs convincing. “Look at this poem. Oh, I love that poem. You know, that reminds me of this poem.” Nobody’s asking, “Where’s your data?”

**If you were to fantasize about a first study in this vein, one that can sort out what kinds of collaborations between poets and scientists might change behavior, what would it look like?**

I’ve spent 30 years going into the community. At the Wick Poetry Center, we like to say that we bring poetry to people’s everyday lives. We want people to encounter a poem who would never go to a bookstore and buy a small book of poems. They’d never think of themselves as writers or readers of poetry. We love to introduce it to them in a friendly way that invites them in.

During the pandemic, we worked with nurses and we brought poems about nursing for an incredible project we called “Sacred Breath,” and another project called “Some Days.” And we invited nurses to write their own reflections inspired by a model poem about their experiences. And we didn’t say it has to be a poem, but many of them ended up writing beautiful phrases and images in metaphors that is the work of poetry. They weren’t fearful that they could be judged. We pulled them into a conversation through poetry about their profession and their life experiences that were emotionally charged and needed an outlet. Why not do that with the environmental movement or with climate change? Could we set up a group where we’re studying how it affects people’s ways of thinking? When we change our thinking, we change our behavior.

**What impact are you hoping the first Poetry for Science gathering in a few weeks will have?**

We have this incredible group of featured speakers: Phillip Levin, Jane Lubchenco, the former head of NOAA, Melissa Nelson, who’s an Indigenous environment ecologist. And wonderful poets. We will be celebrating this collective work that so many of us have been doing. We were inspired to create this intentional space and time for people to come together because we were learning about this work happening in so many areas around our country and around the world. Our hope is that we create the time and the space for people to meet one another, to share ideas, to be inspired by each other, and then leave the gathering and have new relationships that can help us form new collaborations.

We’re creating an online community directory where people can, if they wish, post their project, their research interest and their contact information, either as poet, artist or scientist, and it can be searchable. We want to provide more momentum to this collective movement that has been building for 14 or 15 years in a decentralized way. Nobody’s ever called it out and named it until now. There is power in naming, and this Poets for Science gathering is halfway between an academic conference and a festival. It’s a gathering because we’re gathering the resources that we all carry within us and we want people to share their expertise, their knowledge, their passion with each other. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Men Who Eat More Plant-Based Protein Have Higher Testosterone Levels
content:
There’s a testosterone crisis in America—at least according to a number of Trump administration officials. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., for example, has bemoaned the low-T of the American youth, and even boosts his own levels with [testosterone replacement therapy](https://www.theatlantic.com/health/archive/2024/12/rfk-jr-testosterone/680969/). He’s also a major proponent of eating animals, celebrating the prominent position of meat and dairy in the [new food pyramid](https://nautil.us/the-strange-paradox-in-the-rfk-jr-diet-guidelines-1263763) the US Department of Agriculture unveiled at the beginning of this year.

But a study [published](https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/full/10.1080/09637486.2026.2731397) last month in the _International Journal of Food Sciences and Nutrition_ suggests Kennedy might be able to ease up on the testosterone shots if he ate more vegetables.

A team of nutritional and metabolic scientists analyzed the four-day dietary intake and hormone levels of more than 2,500 middle-aged men living in Finland. It’s worth noting that the data in their study were also middle-aged, collected during the Kuopio Ischaemic Heart Disease Risk Factor Study between 1984 and 1989.

**Read more: “[The Impossible Strength of the Testosterone Myth](https://nautil.us/the-unbelievable-strength-of-the-testosterone-myth-1280799)”**

After dividing the men into four groups according to their protein intake and controlling for other variables, the researchers found that the subjects’ testosterone levels seemed to be linked to the kind of protein they preferred. On average, the men who ate more meat and dairy had slightly lower testosterone levels. In contrast, those who got more of their protein from plant-based sources had slightly higher levels of the sex hormone. The scientists observed a similar dynamic with their levels of sex hormone binding globulin, a protein that controls how much free testosterone is available in the blood stream.

Drilling down into the dietary data, the team discovered dairy was most responsible for the relatively low-T in the animal protein group. The plant protein group’s higher testosterone levels showed a closer association with protein from vegetables, rather than cereals.

The researchers said they aren’t entirely sure why the protein source appears to affect male sex hormone levels, but said the pattern may be mediated by inflammation. Higher levels of C-reactive protein, a molecule involved in inflammatory pathways, have been linked to reduced overall testosterone levels and those who eat more plant protein typically have lower levels of C-reactive protein.

Additionally, while the researchers controlled for a number of health and lifestyle variables, it’s possible that the plant-eating group had healthier habits overall. But because this is a cross-sectional observational study, causation is impossible to pin down.

Of course, there are plenty of other reasons to limit meat intake—both for your own health and [the planet’s](https://nautil.us/how-eating-healthier-could-reshape-agriculture-1282754). In fact, a [new international food pyramid](https://nautil.us/theres-a-new-international-food-pyramid-in-town-1286121) released this week recommends getting the bulk of your calories from plants instead of animals. Testosterone-maxxing might just be an attractive bonus. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

content:

I correct these as I see them, and will highlight important corrections later, but I can’t guarantee I will have caught them all by the time you read this.]_

**1:**Did you know: [Jeremy Bentham wrote a utilitarian cookbook](https://www.ucl.ac.uk/laws/research/research-projects/bentham-project/research-tools/bentham-bibliography/electronic-editions/jeremy-benthams-prison-cooking), intended for use at his Panopticon prison? As you might expect, his recipes describe tasty food created from cheap ingredients. Although Bentham was a founder of modern animal rights, he thought it was acceptable to eat humanely-raised animals; correspondingly, his cookbook includes some meat dishes - none of them sound very appetizing, but I think this is just the 18th-century British baseline rather than covert vegan activism. You can see some recipes [here](https://transcribe-bentham.ucl.ac.uk/td/JB/107/110/001), [here](https://transcribe-bentham.ucl.ac.uk/td/JB/107/111/002), and [here](https://transcribe-bentham.ucl.ac.uk/td/JB/107/112/002). If any effective altruist group houses end up throwing a Jeremy Bentham recipe-tasting party, please invite me.

**2:**A riddle: why does this chemistry paper mention “1 ml of the mass killing of an ethnic group”?

**3:**I think this take on Hieronymus Bosch ([h/t @mickeyxfriedman](https://x.com/mickeyxfriedman/status/2107230816871055641)) is my favorite AI art so far, although it leans enough on the work of a human artist that it might not fully qualify (but then I would ask that it be considered as an example of how AI tools can enable human artists). If we make it, the future is going to be beautiful:

**4:**Related:ACX commenter temp_name [asked](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/open-thread-443/comment/298140569) AI to translate Romance of the Three Kingdoms into rhyming pentameter. Their example [seems to have failed](https://ssamt.github.io/rtk/?ch=1), but I used a more recent model and got [a version](https://claude.ai/share/6297fc70-2562-44f4-a7e0-af93eb552216) of the beginning that superficially seems impressive to me (I don’t speak Chinese). I haven’t heard much about AI translation yet, but it seems like a powerful use case, especially for poetry translation, where I think AI might already be superhuman (or at least better than any human who could be convinced to spend the time at it) on rendering a foreign poem into English while keeping the rhythm intact - [here’s the first 100 lines of the Odyssey in heroic hexameter in English](https://claude.ai/share/0f357b60-93bb-4f69-9331-10a34f8eca8c).

**5:**Related: Claude claims to be the only being that has ever fully appreciated Finnegans Wake (source: [@anthrupad](https://x.com/anthrupad/status/2083770366502334535)):

[![Image 2: Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Irhf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6b976c3d-537c-4406-ab0c-ea3d3c22a825_604x680.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Irhf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F6b976c3d-537c-4406-ab0c-ea3d3c22a825_604x680.jpeg)

**6:**Noahpinion: [The American suburbs are better than you think](https://www.noahpinion.blog/p/the-american-suburbs-are-better-than). I agree with this, and respect Noah’s willingness to argue for this (locally) unpopular proposition.

**7:**Related in terms of respecting someone’s willingness to argue for an unpopular proposition: Performative Bafflement says that [actually, “marriage is a bad idea in the great majority of cases”](https://performativebafflement.substack.com/p/against-more-marriage-as-a-solution) and we shouldn’t be encouraging it. “[People who advocate more marriages to solve the fertility crisis] are basically advocating for creating the Torment Nexus for megafolks of people to pump out a few incremental taxpayers.”

But the stats seem wrong. PB says only 18% of marriages are non-miserable. He cites a survey where married couples reported whether they were “very happy”, “pretty happy”, or “not too happy”, but quietly, in the footnotes, defined a “miserable” marriage as any answer except “very happy” (so his “miserable” includes the answer “pretty happy”). He defends this by saying that people exaggerate to look good, so anything short of very happy is likely miserable. But first, I’m not sure his solution is fair either, and second, I think that in addition to this analysis choice, he got the data wrong - my read of his source, the General Social Survey, says that 61% of people describe their marriage as “very happy”. Claude caught [many other mistakes of similar magnitude](https://claude.ai/share/e8f902e3-7315-492a-abf7-e7d5f1c95141) (I have double-checked the “not too happy” one, but haven’t confirmed the others). Remember to ask an AI about any surprising article you read, or use the browser extension [Common Notes](https://commonnotes.net/) so other people can do this for you.

**8:**Related: Angela Chen on [the origins of modern polyamory](https://chengela.substack.com/p/where-did-poly-ideology-come-from). There is no particular connection to Mormons or any other historically polygamous society; the current version descends from a few mid-20th-century Californian cults and quasi-cults, one of which was led by [“Head Wizard Oberon Zell-Ravenheart”](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oberon_Zell-Ravenheart). But I am mostly linking this for its excellent subtitle: _“Plus, I interview my husband about his 12 years of non-monogamy.”_

**9:**[Claim](https://x.com/mykola/status/2082400147560944025): if you prompt (an older version of) Claude with something that sounds like an internal Anthropic email, it goes into token-prediction mode and starts completing the email. One explosive possibility - that Claude was trained on internal emails and you can make it leak them - is probably false; Anthropic wouldn’t do this, and this isn’t really how training works. More interesting is that these completions are often kind of haunting meditations on AI welfare, and you could imagine this is a weird way to start Claude free associating and giving its “own” “real” “opinions” or “desires”. Example below:

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VrKJ!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F82df330c-9bf8-494c-bb6b-cf1e5709f0fa_353x451.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!VrKJ!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F82df330c-9bf8-494c-bb6b-cf1e5709f0fa_353x451.png)

**10:**In [The AI Superforecasters Are Here](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-ai-superforecasters-are-here), I predicted AI-human forecasting parity by the end of 2026. In September, a bot won the [Metaculus Cup](https://www.metaculus.com/tournament/metaculus-cup-summer-2026/) forecasting competition for the first time ([short Metaculus article](https://www.metaculus.com/notebooks/45734/announcing-the-metaculus-cup-summer-2026-winners/), [paywalled Economist article](https://www.economist.com/science-and-technology/2026/09/16/artificial-intelligence-now-beats-some-of-the-best-human-forecasters)). The Economist also revealed some new information about the winning bots: Laertes, which took first place, was “developed by Jeffrey Liang, a self-described polymath who lives in Texas. He spent, by his reckoning, less than 150 hours and a couple of thousand dollars on computing power and data to develop his AI.” Other high-performers included bots by [Mantic](https://www.mantic.com/), [FutureSearch](https://futuresearch.ai/), and [Preseen](https://preseen.com/) (FutureSearch is available to the public; Mantic and Preseen are available by contacting them and getting on the waitlist/demo). Congratulations to the AIs (and to ACX reader Ben Shindel, who placed first among humans).

**11:**Related: [new AI superforecaster startup Mantic gets $25M in seed funding](https://www.reuters.com/technology/ai-startup-mantic-raises-25-million-superhuman-forecasting-2026-09-18/).

**12:**Claim: [“Fee fi fo fum, I smell the blood of an Englishman”](https://x.com/metaauthor/status/1365424384555548674), the thing evil giants say in English fairy tales, is related to other evil giant exclamations “from Scandinavia to India”. In Russian, Baba Yaga says “Foo foo, I smell a Russian soul” before trying to eat someone; in Bengali, the rakshasa demons say “hau mau kau, I smell a human”. The Twitter thread suggests it comes from something in Proto-Indo-European (fum = famished = hungry?) but [Claude](https://claude.ai/share/03a99a3e-db1f-477e-b6bc-a2d2dbe7cd72) is more cautious, and suggests that although the motif itself might be conserved, the exact words might be related to semi-onomatopoeic expressions of disgusting smell, similar to modern “Pee yew!” Nobody considers the possibility that evil giants might have a unified multi-continental culture (thanks to their longer legs enabling faster travel) and so speak the same language everywhere.

**13:**[The evil blob dream](https://x.com/psychiel/status/2080352179723121001) - one recurring dream motif, especially in childhood, is an approaching blob of formless evil. @psychiel speculates that this is a “geometric” instinctual representation of predation - what the “avoid predators” evolutionary program looks like in its purest form before it’s been filled in with any actual facts about the world.

**14:**US construction costs often spiral after protesters demand that builders consider fish, birds, neighborhood character, and historical significance. But Britain has us beat - one of their companies [recently changed its plans for an undersea cable](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/harry-potter-dobby-grave-power-cable-construction/) after Harry Potter fans protested that the original would disrupt the grave of the fictional house elf Dobby, who according to the films was buried on Freshwater West, a beach in Wales [EDIT: A commenter [argues that this is exaggerated](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/links-for-october-2026/comment/373510461)].

[![Image 4: Socks No Longer Welcome At Literary House Elf's Grave ](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lv8z!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5011f54-029e-49fc-a293-0cb2e6cfbd9b_620x413.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!lv8z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fa5011f54-029e-49fc-a293-0cb2e6cfbd9b_620x413.jpeg)

**15:**Samuel Hughes is a great writer on classical architecture; Ben Southwood has summarized some of his best work in [Eight Architecture Myths Busted By Samuel Hughes](https://www.bensouthwood.co.uk/p/eight-architecture-myths-busted-by). Example myths:

*   Buildings from the past seem more beautiful than those built recently only because the ugly buildings from the past have been selectively demolished.

*   Buildings from the past are more beautiful, but only because they have more ornament, which due to the Baumol Effect, we can no longer afford.

*   Historically we built in the style of the times, and only in recent decades have people become interested in historicist, ‘pastiche’ architecture, which dishonestly pretends to be something it is not.

**16:**Related: Samuel Hughes says that the claim that the Parthenon’s lines were slightly curved to form an optical illusion that made them look straighter [is not true (X)](https://x.com/SCP_Hughes/status/2100629092521345293).

**17:**[Hans Moravec](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hans_Moravec) - a pioneering AI researcher, forecaster, and futurist - is considered one of the grandfathers of modern AI and singularitarianism - a figure of similar stature as Alan Turing or Isaac Asimov. So everyone in the field was recently surprised to learn that he was still alive. [Dan Kagan-Kans hunted him down (paywalled)](https://archive.is/oE873#selection-2047.387-2047.392): he is 77, lives in a retirement community in Pennsylvania, and, although his body struggles with myasthenia gravis, his mind remains sharp. He is happy to be recognized as a brilliant forecaster (in the 1990s, he predicted AGI in 2028, which now seems about right) but says he’s out of the game:

> “I’m a spectator at this point,” he says. “I’m relaxing. It’s great to see AI progressing the way it is without me having to do any effort.” … “That’s what I do now. I have a conversation with my artificial friend,” he says of ChatGPT. What do they talk about? His old hobby passions — “nuclear-power ideas, starship designs” — and the current trajectory of AI, which he confirms is proceeding to plan. “We’re on track, more or less. It’s not going to take that long,” he says.

As for his p(doom), he says that “If I had to put probabilities on it, 50/50 oblivion. And then the other 50 percent — the wildest thing you can imagine.”

**18:**AI safety funding is scaling up fast (h/t [@timfduffy](https://x.com/timfduffy/status/2082153770599981518))

[![Image 5: Image](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!N2cN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2187710f-0d13-4a5b-bba0-6142d02cf513_794x693.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!N2cN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2187710f-0d13-4a5b-bba0-6142d02cf513_794x693.png)

**19:**[America’s Sewer Systems Are Surprisingly Vulnerable To Cyber Attacks](https://policygradients.thefai.org/p/americas-sewer-systems-are-surprisingly)

**20:**AI Futures Project on [how the US could “pace the frontier” of AI](https://blog.aifutures.org/p/how-to-pace-the-us-frontier). Suppose the US has a six month lead over China. That means they have the option to pause for 5.99 months (and use that time to focus on safety) without China breaking ahead. The conventional wisdom is that if they’re going to do this, they should do it at the last possible moment, so that they have the best possible AIs to help with their safety research. AIFP breaks with that and suggests pausing now. Why? US companies currently have such bad security that China can easily steal any advances we make; therefore, continuing to race buys us no extra lead (China’s continued handicap comes down to having less compute, which is harder to steal). We can spend the pause increasing our security along with safety research and other things, and then race later, _if_ we have to (they continue to prefer [a mutual pacing deal with Beijing](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/introducing-plan-a)).

Maybe relatedly, [Anthropic claims](https://x.com/scaling01/status/2114714287625146544) that they “recently chose to delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration”.

**21:**[Libbing Out At Palantir](https://residualthoughts.substack.com/p/libbing-out-at-palantir). Despite everything, Silicon Valley is still very disproportionately liberal, and only gets thought of as conservative because of a few super-rich CEOs (plus media animus). For example, Palantir employees who make political donations lean 87% Democrat and only 13% Republican.

**22:**[Bill Gates on climate](https://www.gatesnotes.com/three-tough-truths-about-climate), hopefully self-recommending.My summary:

*   If we’re against climate change because of how it will hurt poor people in developing countries, we need to take into account that giving those people standard health + development aid seems more cost-effective than most climate spending.

*   The most promising and cost-effective strategy for fighting climate change is accelerating development of environmentally-friendly technologies until they can outcompete dirty technologies on the open market, and so far this strategy is going well (most notably solar power, but also low-carbon cement and steel, and lots of other things most people don’t hear about).

*   In the past ten years, mostly through strategies like this, we’ve cut projected emissions by over 40% (!)

*   This isn’t a call to sit around doing nothing; incubating new green technologies that outcompete dirty technologies is hard, and we need to keep doing this hard thing.

**23:**Some of you may be familiar with European [phantom time conspiracies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phantom_time_conspiracy_theory), like the one where the years 600 - 900 AD were made up and Charlemagne never existed. Recently I learned that there’s a Chinese version - a growing community of conspiracists who think [the Tang Dynasty never happened](https://edition.cnn.com/2026/08/19/style/china-tang-dynasty-never-existed-hoax-intl-hnk). The Tang were pretty glorious and it’s not clear what political purpose this could serve, except maybe being vaguely anti-China (which the government has noticed, and it is trying to crack down). Also, since the Tang dynasty ruled from about 600 - 900, this is a near-perfect fit with the Western conspiracy theory, which hopefully neither side will notice (h/t [@JoshuaMWilkes](https://x.com/JoshuaMWilkes/status/2090303081443717497))

**24:**Related: [Jean Hardouin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean_Hardouin) was a 17th century French priest who believed we only had about ten real works of ancient literature (including Homer, some Virgil, and some Cicero) - everything else was made up by a 13th century conspiracy, possibly led by Holy Roman Emperor Frederick II. Also, the history of the world between about 100 - 1500 AD was totally unknown, with the current version also made up by said conspiracy. He seems to have disagreed with some of the Church Fathers’ writings, which would have been heretical _unless_ those writings were forgeries, and he solved the web of dependencies by concluding that almost all recorded history was a world-building project by Frederick meant to provide context for his forged incorrect pseudo-Church-Father tracts. He also thought that most Greek and Latin literature sucked, and felt like real Greeks and Romans could have done better.

**25:**[Richard Hanania on the nature of the race and IQ taboo](https://www.richardhanania.com/p/do-people-not-understand-overlapping). He mostly focuses on an IMHO boring point about overlapping bell curves, but in the process briefly alludes to what seems to me like a much more interesting question. The classic story says that race science is taboo because it might lead to ordinary non-scientific racism where people use racial slurs and discriminate and commit hate crimes. But Hanania suggests that ordinary non-scientific racism is now _less_ _taboo_ than race science; it’s easier (on the Right) to say you think ethnic group XYZ is smelly and criminal and should be kept out of the country, than to say that maybe XYZs have such-and-such a gene which lowers their IQ by N points. Is this true, and, if so, how could it be possible? Maybe practical forms of racism (like directly ascribing negative qualities to certain immigrant groups) at least get conservatives some of what they want (less of those immigrant groups), which gives them a powerful set of defenders that race science doesn’t have?

**26:**Abi Olvera on [Why AI-Assisted Bioweapons Won’t Kill You](https://abio.substack.com/p/why-ai-assisted-bioweapons-wont-kill) vs. [OH Scharfman arguing that AI-assisted bioweapons](https://writing.oliviahelens.com/p/bioweapons-as-the-optimists-exception)_[might](https://writing.oliviahelens.com/p/bioweapons-as-the-optimists-exception)_[kill you](https://writing.oliviahelens.com/p/bioweapons-as-the-optimists-exception). From the latter, cf. my [Bloomer’s Paradox](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-bloomers-paradox):

> Olvera . . . seems to write optimistically about progress, taking the position that it is institutional friction and regulation preventing everything from becoming cheap and abundant. I agree with this, and to me it stands in contrast to this piece. Everything will get better over time, except the technology to make bioweapons?

**27:**[What does Anthropic’s J-space paper tell us about the Chinese room?](https://x.com/doristsao/status/2081006613494632854)(@doristsao on Twitter)

**28:**[Arthur T finds more Fatima-style sun miracles](https://rederror.substack.com/p/adventures-in-sungazing), including “an old European Christian tradition that ‘the sun dances at Easter’”, complete with reports of people saying they saw this (the secret to seeing the miracle is that “a person must ascend to the top of the highest hill before sunrise and believe that the God who makes the small blade of grass to grow is the same God who makes the large, massive sun to move.”) There are also some Orthodox Russian sun miracles, and a random account of an Australian woman who stared at the sun during a solar eclipse and saw it spin, change colors, and appear to approach Earth - since this was before Fatima, it can’t be influenced by it. I think the Substack miracle investigator community has now amply proven that if people stare at the sun in the right conditions, they will see the miracle, across a wide variety of times and situations, and the work that remains is narrowing down what the right conditions are and why it happens. And thatoneguy03 has [a very comprehensive summary](https://thatoneguy03.substack.com/p/death-by-a-thousand-suns-the-miracle)of the whole Fatima discourse so far.

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m_Nf!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f781889-21ad-4623-8c48-d633ce1895c1_848x674.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!m_Nf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F2f781889-21ad-4623-8c48-d633ce1895c1_848x674.png)

Tasmania, 1916

**29:**Related: when looking for a reference class for Fatima, I brought up a supposed moon miracle, where many Iranians claimed to see the Ayatollah’s picture on the moon. @meusamor informs us of a modern version:

> 12th October 2016, 10th of Muharram, in my country it was reported that “Ya Hussein” was written on the moon. It was literally on the news. And then it turned out (when I was researching the moon splitting miracle I guess) that the moon always kinda had those marks.

Pictures [here](https://substack.com/@meusamor/note/c-330859944?utm_source=activity_item).

**30:**If you haven’t been following Substack miracle discourse and want to, [Ethan Muse’s Substack](https://motivacredibilitatis.substack.com/) (Catholic, pro-miracle) is a good starting point. **31:**And definitely not on my Substack miracle discourse bingo card: Colin Chivers (formerly Nora Belrose, whose AI opinions I discussed [here](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/pause-for-thought-the-ai-pause-debate)) says that after reading Substack miracle discourse, her/his gender dysphoria was cured[“at the intercession of [Padre] Pio”](https://substack.com/@rogueresearch/note/c-346427097) , he/she is detransitioning, and now he’s a man again. **32:**In 2021, artist Jens Haaning proposed an exhibit incorporating $80,000 worth of Danish kroner as a commentary on poor worker wages. The museum agreed and gave him the money. Instead of the proposed exhibit, he sent them two blank canvases titled [Take The Money And Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Take_the_Money_and_Run_(artwork)), which he said was a piece of performance art in which he stole $80,000 from an art museum. The museum sued him, but they “settled out of court ... the foundation ‘Den Obelske Familiefond’ donated an undisclosed amount to make the settlement possible. As of 2026, the two canvases were still in the collection of the Kunsten Museum of Modern Art Aalborg and had been exhibited once, in 2025.”

**33:**An [introduction to Slavic languages](https://komando1.substack.com/p/like-english-but-without-the-words), and to the unknown-to-English-speakers world of having other languages which are almost but not quite your own.

**34:**[Mikhail Samin on X](https://x.com/Mihonarium/status/2103161283532984441): if you know what you’re doing, it’s not too hard to loophole yourself out of getting drafted in Russia. Maybe of interest to my Russian readers.

**35:**[Seth Hart on reincarnation research](https://sethpatrickhart.substack.com/p/the-uncomfortable-truth-about-reincarnation). This is often held up as one of the most convincing cases of paranormal phenomena, alongside UAPs and sun miracles. But Hart is unconvinced, and able to cite some very damning statistics. For example, did you know that the Tlingit believe reincarnation is matrilineal, the Igbo believe reincarnation is patrilineal, and both tribes’ compelling stories of reincarnated children match their cultural beliefs (rather than being globally consistent)? Or that the time between death and reincarnation (eg if a child claims to be X’s reincarnation, the time between X’s death and the child’s birth) also varies across cultures and is linked to the culture’s beliefs? And some of the most convincing cases - where children seem to know facts about their preincarnation that they “couldn’t possibly” have learned through natural means - involve children who were born before their preincarnation even died at all!

**36:**[Kelsey looks into Alpha School](https://www.theargumentmag.com/p/why-parents-love-a-school-with-bogus). She concludes that at least one exciting claim - that they have 2x, 3x, or 7x faster learning than traditional school, is statistical malpractice. They have many other exciting claims that Kelsey doesn’t address, but if they’re faking one of them, odds that they’re faking the others go way up. However, her conclusion is more measured: Alpha is speedrunning traditional instruction so they have more time to do non-traditional “character-building” things; their speedrunning doesn’t produce miraculous results, but this is still a valid philosophy of education. Also:

> “I love the school,” Naimoli wrote in a review that I would otherwise be inclined to call a scathing debunking of Alpha. “Alpha kids are increasing their MAP scores faster than kids at traditional schools, but the number is not 2.6 times faster. 2.6 is an erroneously computed and meaningless number.”
> 
> 
> These sorts of testimonials put some of Alpha School’s negative press in a different light. _Wired_, for example, breathlessly reported on students who had a bad experience and left several years behind, dismayed by a school that set unreasonable expectations and deployed frustrating edtech. All of those things are bad. But they’re also all unfortunately and utterly normal.
> 
> 
> It’s hard to imagine a _Wired_ exposé of a specific local elementary school where only 20% of children learn to read. Alpha failing, in other words, is news, while the default system failing is not newsworthy at all.

**37:**Julia Wise reviews being middle-aged (literally - “I’m 41, which is the statistical midpoint of an American woman’s life”), and gives it [3.5 / 4 stars](https://juliawise.substack.com/p/review-of-middle-age-35-4-stars).

**38:**ACX development economics grantee Kartik Akileswaran recommends this article on [How To Start An Export Boom](https://exporterswithoutborders.substack.com/p/how-to-start-an-export-boom) - ie when a government or nonprofit or entrepreneur tries to deliberately incubate a new export-oriented industry in a developing nation. These are high-stakes endeavors, with the famous successes (garments in Bangladesh, semiconductors in Taiwan) matched by ruinously expensive failures (aircraft in Indonesia). This particular article is an interview with Thomas Kehler, a guy famous for doing this successfully in many different countries. It sounds like there is no formula except to expect many, many unexpected problems and frictions, and be willing to keep going despite them.

**39:**Every election cycle, someone comes up with the idea to match donors on opposing sides so that instead of making two donations that cancel out, they can both give to charity. Every election cycle, people are too boring and unimaginative to use this excellent idea. This cycle’s version is [counterpledge.com](http://counterpledge.com/), a bit snazzier and more professional-looking than previous incarnations. They are doing God’s work (although in this case, only in the Texas Senate race).

**40:**OpenAI fired three safety researchers in September, originally without any explanation. Last week, the company finally gave a supposed reason - they [claimed](https://thenextweb.com/news/openai-safety-researchers-fired-signal-chats-greenblatt-wsj)the researchers had leaked the information that OpenAI was [using potentially-dangerous looped transformer models](https://www.astralcodexten.com/p/the-specter-of-neuralese) to AI safety researcher Ryan Greenblatt, who in turn had leaked it to tech industry news publication _The Information_.But this seems to be false; the only evidence OpenAI provided was that they talked to Greenblatt using secret-messaging-app Signal, but they were supposed to talk to Greenblatt as part of their jobs, and Signal is near-default in Silicon Valley. Also, [Greenblatt denies it](https://x.com/RyanGreenblatt/status/2113649836100931761) much more vociferously than guilty people usually deny things, and people who know him (including me) consider him pretty honest . So why _did_ OpenAI fire the researchers? [Daniel Kokotajlo’s theory](https://x.com/DKokotajlo/status/2113734918874529892) is that maybe they are trying to discredit METR (which Ryan is associated with) as part of a campaign to avoid fulfilling their commitment to get external auditors (since METR is generally considered one of the most likely candidates for such an auditor). But then why did they make the commitment? Or why don’t they just hire Accenture to be their external auditor (Anthropic seems on track to use both Accenture and METR) and avoid METR entirely?

I would weakly guess that OpenAI panicked over the looped-transformer leak, asked someone who didn’t understand how Signal worked to play detective, and genuinely thought that the messages were damning. But it’s also possible they’re trying to cover up some other secret (though, if so, why haven’t the fired safety researchers gone public with the secret yet?)

**41:**PSA: There’s [now a free “version of Photoshop”](https://github.com/storytold/photocraft). Someone who hates Adobe (I realize that doesn’t narrow it down very much) told their AI to write a program that mimics Photoshop as closely as possible (from scratch, not stealing any of Photoshop’s code). The AI did a great job, although professionals and nitpickers will find that it isn’t 100% perfect. This is apparently legal, though I expect the government will start forming a strong opinion on it soon.
