title: A New Map of ‘Empty’ Space Challenges a Tranquil Picture of the Galaxy
content:
For decades, astronomers treated the interstellar medium as a static backdrop to the goings-on of the universe. Now, a wave of 3D mapping is bringing the interstellar medium’s dynamic nature into focus.

![Image 1: Clouds of dust, in browns and reds and bordered by whisps of blues and purples, shimmer against a backdrop dotted with stars.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Mapping-ISM-cr.NASA-Lede-scaled.webp)

In 2010, the Hubble Space Telescope released this image of a pillar of gas and dust in the Carina nebula that’s about 3 light-years — roughly 18 trillion miles — tall.

NASA

## Introduction

You might imagine space to be empty. But the seeming void contains a barely perceptible fog of hydrogen and other neutral atoms. In 2020, NASA’s New Horizons spacecraft, having passed the orbit of Pluto, [measured (opens a new tab)](https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.3847/1538-4357/abb80a) a proxy for the amount of hydrogen around it. In the area between stars in our galaxy — the “interstellar medium,” or ISM — New Horizons found around 130 hydrogen atoms per liter of space.

This hydrogen, along with some helium and other molecules, is mostly left over from the Big Bang, and it’s constantly supplemented by infusions from cosmic phenomena such as stars ejecting jets of gas and dust as they are born and shedding their outer layers as they die.

Because the ISM is so diffuse and changes so slowly, astronomers have largely ignored its details for the last half-century, treating it as a stationary backdrop to the flashier happenings of the universe.

But mostly empty space is less simple than it seems.

Over the past few years, astrophysicists have transformed our understanding of the interstellar medium. Using newly developed maps stretching thousands of light-years across our galaxy, they’ve discovered that it’s not the quiet, steady backdrop that researchers thought. Instead, much of the ISM appears to be unstable — a finding that directly contradicts the leading theoretical models taught in textbooks. The surprise finding could help resolve a long-unanswered question about how quickly stars form.

## **Hot and Cold**

In 1969, the researchers George Field, Donald Goldsmith, and Harm Habing came up with a model of how the ISM behaves. They predicted that it exists in two stable states: cold and warm.

As gas and dust float through space, they pull more gas and dust together through gravity, eventually forming a cloud. These clouds tend to cool down, because fast-moving molecules will collide with other molecules and lose energy. Their temperature stays at a bitter 100 kelvins, or about minus 173 degrees Celsius.

![Image 2: Three enormous smoke-like spires of dust stretch across an expanse of space.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Pillars-of-Creation-cr.NASA_-scaled.webp)

Young stars, which appear red in this 2022 image from the James Webb Space Telescope, form within enormous spires of gas and dust called the Pillars of Creation.

NASA

But sometimes the gas and dust are too hot to collapse into a cold cloud; instead, they form a diffuse one. A diffuse cloud is much more exposed to nearby stars, which deliver new energy in the form of ultraviolet radiation. This process keeps the cloud at a steady temperature near 8,000 kelvins.

Scientists thought that atoms in the interstellar medium would transition to either the cold or warm state almost instantly, leaving basically no unstable, intermediate ISM behind.

In 1977, [Chris McKee (opens a new tab)](https://physics.berkeley.edu/people/faculty/christopher-mckee) and Jeremiah Ostriker [added a third phase (opens a new tab)](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/scan/manifest/1977ApJ...218..148M?art=true) to the picture: At supernova shock fronts, gas could get even hotter, transforming into a scorching plasma at a temperature of half a million kelvins. Yet even in this expanded framework, the atomic gas outside blast zones was assumed to achieve a calm, pressure-balanced existence.

But it was hard to test the theory. Cold atomic hydrogen emits no visible light. The easiest way to measure it is to look for a rare atomic shift: The electron and proton inside a hydrogen atom will sometimes switch between two possible states. This transition emits a faint radio wave at a wavelength of 21 centimeters.

For more than 70 years, astronomers have pointed radio dishes at the sky to detect these whispers of gas, but looking out along a single line of sight from Earth, they can only collect a tangled pile of signals from overlapping clouds. Sorting through the results is like looking through a stack of semitransparent colored plastic sheets; their colors blend together, making it difficult to identify any individual layer.

Only in recent years, with the launch of new space telescopes, have astronomers been able to probe the space between stars in enough detail to pull these layers apart.

## **The Gift of Gaia**

The [Gaia telescope](https://www.quantamagazine.org/gaia-telescopes-first-data-set-released-20160914/), launched in 2013, created new opportunities to understand the ISM by giving scientists access to a 3D map of the stars around our sun.

You can see one method it used to make this map by holding your thumb in front of your face and closing your left eye, then your right. If you switch back and forth, you’ll notice that your thumb seems to move relative to whatever is behind it. The closer your thumb is to your face, the more your view of it will change. This phenomenon is called parallax.

![Image 3: In a room with a yellow floor, eight scientists in lab coats and hairnets watch as a sunshield unfolds around a cylindrical spacecraft.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Deployment_of_Gaia-cr.ESA_M.-Pedoussaut-2013.webp)

Scientists test Gaia’s deployable sunshield during the spacecraft’s construction. Gaia operated between 2013 and 2025, and scientists are still analyzing its data.

ESA/M. Pedoussaut, 2013

Gaia observed almost 2 billion stars from different angles as the Earth moved from one side of the sun to the other during its yearly orbit. Studying the effects of parallax allowed researchers to determine the stars’ distances from Earth.

Scientists then studied how the light from those stars dimmed and reddened as it traveled through the ISM on its way to Gaia. By collecting this data from a variety of angles, and by using the distance information they’d gathered through parallax, scientists were able to build up a better understanding of the density of the dust between stars.

But turning that information into a 3D map of the ISM was not straightforward. Many possible configurations of the ISM could satisfy the same data, said [Gregory Green (opens a new tab)](https://en.westlake.edu.cn/faculty/gregory-green.html), an astronomer at Westlake University in Hangzhou, China. More data offered the astronomers better constraints, but it also complicated their calculations. The challenge, Green said, is picking out the most physically plausible arrangement when the underlying math “becomes impossible.”

Over the last decade, Green and other researchers built advanced statistical frameworks to tackle the calculation. In 2024, a separate team used these tools to create a [continuous three-dimensional map (opens a new tab)](https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2024/05/aa47628-23/aa47628-23.html) of the density of the ISM’s dust inside a sphere more than 4,000 light-years wide around our sun.

![Image 4: On a 3D grid, opaque blue clumps are surrounded by transparent yellow clumps.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Map-cr.paper_-scaled.webp)

On this 3D map, unstable gas, depicted in yellow tones, wraps around more stable clumps of dust, depicted in blue. The small yellow dot in the center is our sun.

The dust map showed researchers where interstellar dust was concentrated, revealing the dense clouds scattered through the space between stars. But it couldn’t tell them how hot or cold that dust was. To understand the full range of ISM temperatures, researchers would need a second map to reveal how it gets heated. That map would come from an unlikely source.

## **State of Flux**

Jonathan Shelest, an undergraduate at the Technion in Haifa, Israel, remembers an astrophysics research seminar in 2024, when [Shmuel Bialy (opens a new tab)](https://sbialy.wixsite.com/astro), his professor, showed the students images of the gas and dust that gather into billowing structures such as the Pillars of Creation in the voids between stars. “I like to imagine the geometry of everything,” Shelest said. “It was only natural to start imagining all the dynamics, all the structure, all the beauty, and the richness.”

Right after the lecture, Shelest emailed Bialy, asking to join his research group. In an act of kismet, Bialy had recently been looking for a student to explore the ISM through three-dimensional mapping, and so a research partnership was born.

![Image 5: A man with a beard stands in front of a blackboard full of equations](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Shmuel-Bialy-cr.TK_.webp)

Shmuel Bialy, a professor at the Technion in Haifa, Israel, showed students images of the interstellar medium in class.

Courtesy of Shmuel Bialy

Shelest already had the map of the ISM’s dust. The plan was to combine that map with a map of the ultraviolet radiation that heats the ISM up.

By chance, Bialy located just such a map by striking up a conversation at a conference with the astrophysicist [Troy Porter (opens a new tab)](https://profiles.stanford.edu/troy-porter) of Stanford University, who had made a map but had yet to publish it.

So Shelest, Bialy, and their colleagues set out to combine the 200 gigabytes of data in the two maps. At every point in space, they compared the density of the dust with the intensity of the radiation to understand where the ISM was hot and where it was cool. Eventually, they were able to combine the dust and radiation information on a three-dimensional grid.

Shelest then set out to see what the map could tell him. The biggest surprise came when he investigated the ISM’s overall temperature: Shelest found that 27% of the ISM in our galactic neighborhood was cold, 32% was warm, and the remaining 41% sat squarely in the forbidden zone as unstable medium. “I thought I was wrong,” Shelest said. “How do you go to your science adviser and tell him that you get so much unstable media?”

![Image 6: A man with a backpack stands in front of relief carvings outdoors.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Jonathen-Shelest-cr.TK_-1.webp)

Jonathan Shelest, a student at the Technion, found the interstellar medium to be more unstable than expected.

Sophia Leiderman

But the map didn’t appear to be broken. Shelest saw no evidence of artifacts or random statistical noise in the 3D grid. Instead, the unstable ISM formed massive, coherent blankets that wrapped around the cold clouds completely.

All that midrange medium, neither hot nor cold, implies that the older theory is incomplete, said [Adam Ginsburg (opens a new tab)](https://astro.ufl.edu/directory/adam-ginsburg/), an astronomer at the University of Florida. “Something is taking material that should, by the static theory, be sitting in one of these other two states, and it’s stirring it up so that it’s being forced to change states.”

[Desika Narayanan (opens a new tab)](https://www.desikanarayanan.com/), an astrophysicist at the University of Florida, uses an organic metaphor. “Just like your blood in your body is going to have metabolic waste or oxygen in it, and it’s moving different things to different places,” he said, “the ISM is doing the same thing, but with energy, and it’s constantly in a state of flux.”

## **A Measured Approach**

On the July day in 2026 that the group [posted the paper (opens a new tab)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.15352), Shelest’s inbox filled with messages from excited astronomers and requests to collaborate. Still, researchers urge caution before we rewrite the textbooks.

The model could have overestimated the amount of unstable ISM if cold and warm sections were too close together for the model to tell them apart, McKee said. Alternatively, the method the team used to calculate the overall distribution of gas and dust could have led them astray, said [Philipp Frank (opens a new tab)](https://www.ph-frank.de/), an astrophysicist at the Kavli Institute for Particle Astrophysics and Cosmology at Stanford. The researchers used an “ensemble-averaged mean,” a calculation that naturally tends to smooth over sharp contrasts. If a cold cloud transitioned abruptly to a warm one, this method would artificially soften its steep drop in density into a more gradual slope, which would inflate the amount of unstable ISM.

Shelest and Bialy — whose analysis is currently undergoing peer review — acknowledge that limited resolution and map smoothing are both issues, but they argue that mathematical blurring alone cannot account for the majority of the unstable ISM. When the authors tested their modeling on an entirely different dust map with lower resolution, the unstable fraction shifted by only about 5%, they said.

## **The Churn of Creation**

Galaxies are remarkably inefficient at taking raw material —gas and dust —and turning it into stars. For decades, simulations have struggled to explain why. The new map suggests an answer: Star formation is suppressed by the constant cycle of heating and cooling that churns the ISM.

“The reason why star formation is very inefficient is that feedback heats up and pushes on the surrounding gas,” said [Anna Rosen (opens a new tab)](https://anna-rosen.com/), an astrophysicist at San Diego State University. That churning could explain why classic models, which assume that the ISM is in a tranquil equilibrium, don’t quite seem to match reality. Rosen said the models give us “physically grounded snapshots” — unchanging images of patches of hot and cold ISM — “but in between those snapshots, there’s still a lot going on.”

![Image 7](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/JOW-S5-E11-cr.Chanelle-Nibbelink-HP-NO-LOGO-1720x729.webp)

title: When Your Parents Are Dying: Some of the Simplest, Most Difficult and Redemptive Life-Advice You’ll Ever Receive
content:
[![Image 1: When Your Parents Are Dying: Some of the Simplest, Most Difficult and Redemptive Life-Advice You’ll Ever Receive](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/takemyadvice_harmon.jpg?fit=320%2C495&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Take-My-Advice-Letters-Generation/dp/1416578358/?tag=braipick-20)

“Your children are not your children. They are the sons and daughters of Life’s longing for itself,” Kahlil Gibran wrote in his [poignant verse on parenting](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/09/09/on-children-kahlil-gibran/). And yet we are, each of us, someone’s child — physiologically or psychologically or both — and they sing themselves through us as we sing ourselves into our longing for life, whether we like the melody or not.

Like a Zen koan, this fact becomes utterly discomposing when you begin thinking deeply about the fundamental, layered realities beneath the mundane, even banal factuality of the fact. Parents — the very notion of them. The notion that you — this immensely complex totality of sinew and selfhood, this portable universe shimmering with a million ideas and passions and little ways of being-in-the-world that make you you — began as a glimmer in someone else’s eye, a set of chemical reactions that became molecules that became cells in someone else’s body before they constellated into you. The notion that so many dimensions of your personhood, so many of the givens you take for granted in making sense of the world, were forged by someone other than yourself (and possibly other than the body that begot the cells that became you) — someone who occupies, in the cosmogony of you, this strange and staggering position of arbiter between the existence and nonexistence of the particular you that you are.

[![Image 2](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/11/Lily_by_MariaPopova.jpg?resize=680%2C850&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/kinship6212122_print?curator=brainpicker)

_Kinship_ by Maria Popova. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/kinship6212122_print?curator=brainpicker).)

The doubly discomposing experience of what happens when that arbiter crosses the threshold of their own nonexistence is what **Mary Gaitskill** addresses in her thoughtful, tender contribution to [**_Take My Advice: Letters to the Next Generation from People Who Know a Thing or Two_**](https://www.amazon.com/Take-My-Advice-Letters-Generation/dp/1416578358/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](http://www.worldcat.org/title/take-my-advice-letters-to-the-next-generation-from-people-who-know-a-thing-or-two/oclc/49322746&referer=brief_results)) — the wondrous 2002 anthology by artist and writer James L. Harmon, inspired by one of his own spiritual parents: Rilke and his timeless [_Letters to a Young Poet_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/06/29/rilke-letters-to-a-young-poet-macy-barrows/).

Gaitskill writes:

> My advice here is very specific and practicable. It is advice I wish someone had given me as forcefully as I’m about to give it now: When your parents are dying, you should go be with them. You should spend as much time as you can. This may seem obvious; you would be surprised how difficult it can be. It is less difficult if you have a good relationship with the parent or, even if you don’t, if you’re old enough to have lost friends and to have seriously considered your own death. Even so, it may be more difficult than you think.

With the sensitive caveat that there exist people “to whom this general directive does not apply” and her advice is not meant as a rebuke to those people, Gaitskill addresses those of us raised by fallible parents who, in one way or another, failed dreadfully at the deepest task of parenting — unconditional love:

> If you’re a young person who has had a bad relationship with your parent, it’s a nightmare of anger, confusion, and guilt. Even if you hate them, you may still not want to believe it’s happening… Even if your parents have been abusive, physically or emotionally, they are part of you in a way that goes beyond personality or even character. Maybe “beyond” isn’t the right word. They are part of you in a way that runs beneath the daily self. They have passed an essence to you. This essence may not be recognizable; your parents may have made its raw matter into something so different than what you have made of it that it seems you are nothing alike. That they have given you this essence may be no virtue of theirs — they may not even have chosen to do so. (It may not be biological either; all I say here I would say about adoptive as well as birth parents.)

[![Image 3](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2020/07/thestuffofstars10.jpg)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/07/01/the-stuff-of-stars-bauer-holmes/)

Art by Ekua Holmes from [_The Stuff of Stars_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/07/01/the-stuff-of-stars-bauer-holmes/) by Marion Dane Bauer.

Being with a dying parent, Gaitskill notes, is a way of honoring the fact — so basic yet so incomprehensible a fact — that they will soon be gone, and with them will go your experience of being their child in the way you have known, a fundamental way in which you have known yourself. At the heart of this dual recognition is “the hard truth that we know nothing about who we are or what our lives mean.” She writes:

> Nothing makes this plainer than being in the presence of a dying person for any length of time. Death makes human beings seem like very small containers that are packed so densely we can only be aware of a fraction of what’s inside us from moment to moment. Being in the presence of death can break you open, disgorging feelings that are deeper and more powerful than anything you thought you knew. If you have had a loving, clear relationship with your parent, this experience probably won’t be quite as wrenching. There may in fact be moments of pure tenderness, even exaltation. But you might still have to watch your parent appear to break, mentally and physically, disintegrating into something you can no longer recognize. In some ways this is terrible — many people find it absolutely so. There is another side to it, though: In witnessing this seeming breakage, we are glimpsing the part of our parents that doesn’t translate in human terms, that which we know nothing about, and which the human container is too small to give shape to.

[![Image 4](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/03/downadownderry_dorothylathrop2.jpg?resize=680%2C698&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/art-by-dorothy-lathrop-for-down-adown-derry-by-walter-de-la-mare-19224642729_print?curator=brainpicker)

Art by [Dorothy Lathrop](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/03/09/dorothy-lathrop-down-adown-derry/), 1922. (Available [as a print](https://society6.com/product/art-by-dorothy-lathrop-for-down-adown-derry-by-walter-de-la-mare-19224642729_print?curator=brainpicker).)

Because any emotional experience we have when facing another is always an emotional experience we have within, and about, ourselves — especially if that other gave rise to this self — facing this supraknowable quality is facing the limits of our own self-knowledge. Gaitskill writes:

> Knowing your feelings is hard too because there’s so much emotion, it’s hard to tell which is truest. Part of you might want to leave right away; part of you might want to stay forever. That’s why I advised that you stay “for as long as you can.” What that means will vary with each person, with the needs of the parent and the other relations. A day might be enough, or it might take a whole month. If it’s a prolonged situation, it might be good to leave for a few days and come back. Those decisions are so personal they are beyond the scope of my advice — except my advice to pay close attention to yourself. If you feel, _To hell with this, I’m getting out_, don’t worry — there’s room for that. Maybe in fact you should leave. But before you do, be sure that voice is not shouting down a truer one. When your parents die, you will never see them again. You might think you understand that, but until it happens, you don’t.

In a sentiment on the surface contradictory but in fact consonant with the deeper meaning of what artist Louise Bourgeois inscribed into her lifelong diary in her old age — [_“You are born alone. You die alone. The value of the space in between is trust and love.”_](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/04/15/louise-bourgeois-solitude/) — Gaitskill concludes:

> They say that you come into the world alone and that you leave alone too. But you aren’t born alone; your mother is with you, maybe your father too. Their presence may have been loving, it may have been demented, it may have been both. But they were with you. When they are dying, remember that. And go be with them.

Complement this fragment of [**_Take My Advice_**](https://www.amazon.com/Take-My-Advice-Letters-Generation/dp/1416578358/?tag=braipick-20) — which also includes novelist Richard Powers on [the most important attitude you can take toward your life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/09/12/richard-powers-advice/) and philosopher Martha Nussbaum on [how to honor your inner world](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/10/12/martha-nussbaum-take-my-advice/) — with Richard Dawkins on [the luckiness of death](https://www.themarginalian.org/2021/07/25/richard-dawkins-death/), Marcus Aurelius on [embracing mortality as the key to living fully](https://www.themarginalian.org/2019/05/20/marcus-aurelius-meditations-mortality-presence/), and Zen Hospice Project founder Frank Ostaseski on [the five life-redeeming invitation to extend in facing death](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/10/09/the-five-invitations-frank-ostaseski/), then revisit this [tender illustrated meditation on the cycle of life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/05/03/and-so-it-goes-paloma-valdivia/).
